topic: Brief Claude like a new colleague: the five parts of a good brief instead of one-line prompts
audience: Professionals who use Claude at work and get generic first answers
goal: Write their next request as a five-part brief, using the free guide on mojeedabisiga.com/learn
notes: From the guide Brief Claude like a new colleague: a one-line prompt leaves Claude to fill in everything you didn't say, so it picks the safe, middle-of-the-road answer written for nobody in particular. Every detail you add replaces a guess with a fact.

The five parts: the goal (what it's for, not just the task), the background (who it's for, what they know, what happened), the material (paste or attach the notes, numbers, draft), the shape (length, format, tone, order), the finish line (what done means, and what to do if something's missing: list it instead of guessing).

Example: one line 'Write me a report on our Ghana sales.' vs a brief: help the board decide whether to keep selling in Ghana; they meet Friday, have seen last quarter's numbers, two members want to pull out; work only from the attached sheet; one page, three options (stay, shrink, pull out) each with cost and main risk, recommendation at the top, plain English; done when every number comes from the sheet; list anything missing at the end instead of guessing.
Ask me first prompt: 'Before you start, ask me the five questions you most need answered to do this well. Wait for my answers.'
Show what good looks like: paste a past example ('Match this format'); one example beats a paragraph of adjectives.
Correct like feedback, not a fresh start: say what to change and why ('Shorter, because the board reads this on their phones').
Save briefs you reuse: custom instructions, a project or a skill (the guide Skill, project, instructions or connector? picks which).
Mojeed's free guides are at https://mojeedabisiga.com/learn (the pages are listed in learn_catalog.json).
